messages.body_plain:
Sorry again for delays.  A good model of nimble developers will correctly conclude we don't have as much time to respond here as we'd like, but please keep the questions coming.

I agree matrix2mv is not very clear.  It's not even exported.  I've just filed a github issue for us to improve usability of modelValues objects.  Meanwhile, here is an example that I think should get you going.  It illustrates running an mcmc, extracting samples, then directly putting them into a new mcmc (as if you're in a new R session).  You should be able to run WAIC from there.

library(nimble)

toyModel <- nimbleModel(
    nimbleCode({
        a ~ dnorm(0,1)
        for(i in 1:2) x[i] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
    })
)

toyMCMC <- buildMCMC(toyModel)

CtoyModel <- compileNimble(toyModel)
CtoyMCMC <- compileNimble(toyMCMC, project = toyModel)
CtoyMCMC$run(50)

samples <- as.matrix(CtoyMCMC$mvSamples)
samplesList <- as.list(CtoyMCMC$mvSamples) # another way to store samples

## Illustrate use of matrix2mv to set first two rows to zero
emptySamples <- samples[1:2,]
emptySamples[1:2, 1:3] <- 0
emptySamples
# matrix2mv only resizes CtoyMCMC$mvSamples if it needs to be longer.
# It doesn't shorten it.
nimble:::matrix2mv(emptySamples, CtoyMCMC$mvSamples)
as.matrix(CtoyMCMC$mvSamples)[1:2,]

# Make a fully independent object, as if we've restarted R
toyModel2 <- nimbleModel(
    nimbleCode({
        a ~ dnorm(0,1)
        for(i in 1:2) x[i] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
    })
)

toyMCMC2 <- buildMCMC(toyModel2)
CtoyModel2 <- compileNimble(toyModel2)
CtoyMCMC2 <- compileNimble(toyMCMC2, project = toyModel2)
CtoyMCMC2$run(1) # I am adding this defensively, to run initializations
nimble:::matrix2mv(samples, CtoyMCMC2$mvSamples)
as.matrix(CtoyMCMC2$mvSamples)

messages.subject: BYM model mixing
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I fitted a BYM model in Nimble (I put the code below) but is not mixing well (it seems that mu and sigmau of my model are correlated, when one goes up the other goes down. It seems also that ICAR and unstructured residuals are correlated). I tried the following to improve my model but it doesn't improve the mixing:
1. centering the unstructured residual
2. Blocking mu and sigmau (I'm not sure if this is correct)

I would appreciate any suggestion, idea to improve my model.
Thanks!

My code:
code <- nimbleCode({
  # priors
  sigmau ~ dunif(0, 10)
  sigmav ~ dunif(0, 10)
  tauu <- 1 / sigmau^2
  mu ~ dflat()

  x[1:N] ~ dcar_normal(adj[1:L], weights[1:L], num[1:N], tauu, zero_mean = 0)

for(i in 1:N) {
    lambda[i] <- expected[i] * exp(mu+x[i]+v[i])
    y[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i])
    v[i] ~ dnorm(mu.v, sigmav)  # centered random effects
  }
  mu.v ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)   # centered random effects
})

set.seed(1)
nregions <- 540
expected <- Exp.muni
y <- Obs.muni
constants <- list(N = nregions, L = length(VR.wb$adj),
                  adj = VR.wb$adj, weights = VR.wb$weights, num = VR.wb$num,
                  expected = expected)
data <- list(y = y)
inits <- list(mu = rnorm(1), sigmau = runif(1,0,10), sigmav = runif(1,0,10), x = rnorm(nregions),
              mu.v=0, v = rnorm(540))

model <- nimbleModel(code, constants = constants, data = data, inits = inits)

cmodel <- compileNimble(model)

conf <- configureMCMC(model, monitors = c('sigmau', 'sigmav', 'mu', 'x', 'v'))
MCMC <- buildMCMC(conf)
cMCMC <- compileNimble(MCMC, project=cmodel)
samples <- runMCMC(cMCMC, niter = 10000, nburnin = 1000, nchains=1)

messages.subject: Re: BYM model mixing
messages.body_plain:
To follow up on Alison's helpful comment...

dcar_normal (when zero_mean = 0, which is the default) implicitly contains a non-zero mean. This is because the ICAR model is an improper model with an flat prior on the mean. So your model looks overparameterized - the x[] vector has an implicit mean, plus you have 'mu', and you have 'mu.v'. I think only one of those three is identified.  My suggestion is to remove both 'mu' and 'mu.v' (i.e., set them to zero) and leave only the mean implicit in 'x'.

You may still find that the 'x' and the 'v' values trade off. The ICAR model tends to give fairly non-smooth spatial values, which makes it hard for the data to distinguish what is 'x' and what is in 'v'. This will probably also mean that sigmav and tauu trade off. I don't know a good solution for this.

However, some possibilities to consider:

1) reparameterize from {sigmav, tauu} to a parameter for the total variance and a parameter for the proportion of that variance that is unstructured.
2) perhaps have lambda be distributed gamma or use a negative binomial for y such that you are basically integrating v out of the model (though you would no longer be assuming v is normally distributed), but still centering the observations on the combination of the ICAR and the expected.

-Chris

messages.body_plain:
hi Hou-Cheng,

It looks like this is producing a segmentation fault, which occurs when NIMBLE's auto-generated C++ code tries to write to some memory address beyond the length of a vector.

In the code that you shared with me in a separate email, I see this:

piFun <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(r = double(1), rcumsum = double(1)) {
    rlength <- length(r)
    prob <- rep(0, rlength)
    i <- 1
    while (rcumsum[i] < 1) {
      prob[i] <- r[i]
      i <- i + 1
    }
    prob[i] <- 1 - sum(r[1:(i-1)])
    returnType(double(1))
    return(c(prob,i))
  }
)

The danger in having a while loop like this is that the code could end up in a situation, depending on the values in 'r', that the code tries to access elements of
r and of rcumsum beyond the extent of those vectors, e.g., rcumsum[rlength+1], and trying to modify prob[i] for i > rlength.  I see in your code that the elements of
r are being generated from rexp(), which doesn't constrain the elements to add to 1 for a fixed number of elements. So I think this is arising only sometimes in
the execution of your code, because it is rare that the code goes beyond the extent of the vector.

So you'll need to add some checking to your piFun to make sure that you never go beyond the length of the vectors.

Side note: even if 'r' were created in such a way that the elements add to 1, because of the limited precision of double-precision floating point numbers,

Dear Zoe,

It's been some time and I went over what you've described in these messages.  Are you still stuck?

It's true that runMCMC calls mcmc$run.  It then does some post-processing of results.  The error you are seeing from runMCMC but not mcmc$run indicates the problem is in the post-processing, possibly arising from NAs in the posterior sample.  If the error from runMCMC goes away when you do not monitor X, then I would guess X is not mixing.  In this case, turning off the monitor for X would hide the problem, allowing runMCMC to finish, but it would not really solve the problem.  If you use mcmc$run directly (and then extract samples using as.matrix(mcmc$mvSamples) ), you could inspect the samples.  This might help one see what the problem is.

If you are still stuck, can you send a fully reproducible example, with any data files needed, on- or off-list, reduced in complexity if at all possible?

-Perry

> To follow up on Alison's helpful comment...
>
> dcar_normal (when zero_mean = 0, which is the default) implicitly contains a non-zero mean. This is because the ICAR model is an improper model with an flat prior on the mean. So your model looks overparameterized - the x[] vector has an implicit mean, plus you have 'mu', and you have 'mu.v'. I think only one of those three is identified.  My suggestion is to remove both 'mu' and 'mu.v' (i.e., set them to zero) and leave only the mean implicit in 'x'.
>
> You may still find that the 'x' and the 'v' values trade off. The ICAR model tends to give fairly non-smooth spatial values, which makes it hard for the data to distinguish what is 'x' and what is in 'v'. This will probably also mean that sigmav and tauu trade off. I don't know a good solution for this.
>
> However, some possibilities to consider:
>
> 1) reparameterize from {sigmav, tauu} to a parameter for the total variance and a parameter for the proportion of that variance that is unstructured.
> 2) perhaps have lambda be distributed gamma or use a negative binomial for y such that you are basically integrating v out of the model (though you would no longer be assuming v is normally distributed), but still centering the observations on the combination of the ICAR and the expected.

Hi Perry,

Thank
you for checking in. Unfortunately, we have yet to solve these issues.

Inspection
of the posterior samples (through mcmc$mvSamples) didn’t help us
identify the problem, as it seemed that the samples had produced
meaningful values. Additionally, MCMC diagnostic (specifically the Gelman-Rubin
statistic and and Geweke Z score) indicated convergence post 80 000 runs, whilst visual inspections of the trace and density plots of monitored parameters
don’t reveal any glaring issues.

We also
explored the possibility of a data set up issue by manually constructing the
required detection histories, as opposed to relying on the custom function
created by Ponisio in her paper. This did now have a meaningful impact. We’ve
also tried to run the model prior to compiling it, to check if C++ was causing
any issues, but again, this has not impacted on the error.

Our team is rather stumped, so we would gladly provide our
simplified code and data (off-list/privately), and welcome any further advice.

Regards,
Zoe

The error you are seeing from runMCMC but not mcmc$run indicates the problem is in the post-processing, possibly arising from NAs in the posterior sample.  If the error from runMCMC goes away when you do not monitor X, then I would guess X is not mixing.  In this case, turning off the monitor for X would hide the problem, allowing runMCMC to finish, but it would not really solve the problem.  If you use mcmc$run directly (and then extract samples using as.matrix(mcmc$mvSamples) ), you could inspect the samples.  This might help one see what the problem is.

messages.body_plain:
John, thanks for your message.  The error was being triggered in some of the internal processing that takes place fo CAR nodes, but the root of the trouble is in your model specification.  In your model, you have the line:

 t[i] <- rbinom(1,1,p1[i])+1

I understanding it's tempting to use this construct in a model, to have t[i] be a valid binary indexing variable (taking values 1 or 2) used to index mu[].  However, as written, this won't function as you intend.  This becomes a deterministic node in NIMBLE (because of the <- assignment), which means the model functions simulate() and calculate() won't calculate densities for this node, as we'd want, and not to mention it threw off the internal processing that takes place with CAR nodes.

I tried replacing your code, you can choose a better variable name than I did, but replacing the line shown above with the two new lines:

tTEMP[i] ~ dbinom(size = 1, prob = p1[i])
t[i] <- tTEMP[i] + 1

Now, tTEMP is a stochastic node, and t[] is a derived deterministic node, which can be used as an index for mu[].  The other change you need to make is in the initial values list, to no longer provide an initial value for t[] (initial values for t[] will be deterministically calculated automatically), and instead add an initial value for tTEMP.  I used:

inits <- list(...., tTEMP = rep(0,N))

With this change, I think it all runs fine now.

Your issue raises an interesting point, about usage of random simulation functions (e.g., rbinom) inside model code, which we may not be clear about in the user manual.

Let me know if this works for you,
Daniel
